Subject: Denis, please stop the sale and talk to me

Denis,

I have tried to write this several times, and each time I have been too angry to finish. I am still angry. But you are my brother, and I want you to hear this from me, clearly, before we do any more damage to each other.

On Thursday at six in the morning, I was shaping baguettes when a photographer from the real estate agency walked into my shop. He told me you had said I was okay with him being there to take pictures.

I had no idea what he was talking about.

That is how I found out you were putting Papa’s building on the market. Not from a conversation with you. Not even from a message warning me what you intended to do. From a stranger with a camera, standing in the bakery while I was working. Karine had to calm me down. I was furious, embarrassed, and trying to understand what was happening in front of my employee.

Afterward, I found the listing on Centris. $1,150,000. Our building, on the market, without us having agreed on it.

I keep thinking about what you said after Maman’s funeral: “No rush, we decide together.”

Together, Denis. Those were your words. I believed you. Now I am trying to understand how we went from that promise to a photographer telling me I had supposedly agreed to something I knew nothing about.

Since Maman died in February, we have had enough to deal with. The estate was settled in August. The building is now half yours and half mine. I know your half belongs to you, and I know you have the right to want something different from what I want. I am not asking you to pretend you have no financial interests or to leave your money tied up forever because I work downstairs.

But my half matters too. So does the business I have spent 31 years running there. This needed a conversation between us before an agent was involved, before a price appeared online, and certainly before anyone was sent into my workplace.

In September, I told you on the phone that I wanted to buy your half. I told you the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. That was a serious offer, not something I said out of emotion and then forgot about. I had gone to the caisse because I was trying to find a way for you to receive your money and for me to keep the bakery.

I understand that $410,000 is not half of the asking price on that listing. We need to talk honestly about that difference. We can discuss the value of the building, what you expect, and whether there is a way to make an agreement work. I cannot promise money I do not have. But I deserved an answer to what I proposed. If you thought it was not enough, why did you not call me and say so?

You may think that, for me, this is all about Papa and Maman. Of course they are part of it. Papa bought that three-storey building on rue Saint-Hubert in 1979. The bakery downstairs, the two apartments upstairs—we both know the place in a way no buyer ever will. I remember how much you loved sleeping in the flour sacks room in the back when we were children, when Papa let you. You have memories there too, even if your life is in Calgary now.

But this is not only about memories.

There are six employees whose jobs depend on this bakery. There are customers who have been coming for years, some for most of the 31 years I have been there. There is the work I do every day, starting before most people are awake. At 57, I cannot treat the possibility of losing my premises as a small inconvenience and simply start again somewhere else.

I pay $2,400 a month in rent to the estate, and I have never been late once. In 2019, I paid $38,000 of my own money for the new roof. That roof protected the whole building, not just my shop. I am not bringing this up to claim that everything belongs to me. I am bringing it up because I have taken real financial responsibility for this place. I need that to be acknowledged when we discuss what happens next.

My lease ends on April 30, 2027. That is close enough that I need answers now. I do not know who will buy the building or what they will want to do with it. That uncertainty is frightening. What happens if a developer wants to redevelop it or turn it into condos? What happens if I am faced with rent I cannot afford? If my rent doubles, the bakery cannot survive it.

You may see a property sale. I have to think about whether I will still have a place to work, whether my employees will still have their jobs, and what becomes of everything I have built.

The way I found out made all of that worse. I felt pushed aside in a decision about something we own together. And hearing that you had told the photographer I was okay with it made me feel that my agreement had been taken for granted—or spoken for—without anyone asking me.

I do not know exactly what you told the agent. I want you to explain it to me. But please make it clear immediately that I have not agreed to photography, visits, or other arrangements inside the bakery. Nobody should be sent into my shop on the understanding that I have given permission when I have not.

What I am asking you to do now is take the building off the market this week so we can have the discussion we should already have had.

If you will not do that, then at the very least I want us to agree, in writing, that I will have the first opportunity to buy your half before you move ahead with anyone else. We can get proper advice about how to put that in place and give ourselves a clear timetable to work through the price and financing. I am not asking for an endless delay. I am asking for a genuine chance to reach an agreement with you before this goes further.

Please call me this week. I want to speak to you, not receive a text through your wife. This is not an attack on her, and I do not want to put her in the middle. You and I need to hear each other directly. If we are going to settle this, we have to be able to talk as brother and sister, even when the conversation is difficult.

I want to understand what you need and why you have done this. I also need you to listen to what this means for me without dismissing it as sentimentality. I am frightened about the bakery, and I am deeply hurt by you. Both are true.

I have been angry enough to think of saying things I could never take back. I am trying not to do that, because I do not hate you. I love you. That is part of why this hurts so much. I expected a difficult conversation about the building might come. I did not expect to learn about it from a stranger at six in the morning.

We have already lost Papa and Maman. I do not want to lose my brother over this too. But we cannot protect our relationship by pretending that what happened was acceptable or by letting the sale continue while I am left trying to catch up.

Please stop this long enough for us to talk properly. Call me yourself. Tell me what happened, tell me what you want, and give me a fair chance to buy your half.

You said we would decide together. I am asking you to keep that promise.
